newsitem.title: USA: U.S. phone group asks FCC to reject SBC bid now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. phone group asks FCC to reject SBC bid now.

text.p: A phone industry group urged regulators Wednesday to reject immediately SBC Communications Inc's bid to offer long-distance service.

The Association for Local Telecommunications Services (ALTS) also called on the Federal Communications Commission to penalize SBC for alleged "blatant misrepresentations" in its long-distance application.

ALTS, which represents companies offering local service in competition with the Baby Bells, told the FCC that SBC does not face competition for residential local phone service in Oklahoma, where the San Antonio, Texas-based parent of Southwestern Bell is seeking to offer long-distance calling.

Under last year's telecom law, SBC and other Baby Bells in general must show they face competition from another carrier offering business and residential phone service before winning FCC approval to enter the $80 billion long-distance business.
"You can't pick up the phone in Oklahoma and get competitive residential local service," Richard Metzger, an attorney for ALTS, told a news conference.

In its FCC filing, ALTS contended that SBC knew when it submitted its long-distance application that Brooks Fiber Properties Inc was not offering residential service in Oklahoma -- contrary to what SBC said in its application.

"Despite the fact that Brooks expressly informed SBC that Brooks did not provide residential service, SBC nonetheless completely and intentionally misrepresented the facts by claiming that Brooks was providing residential service," said Brooks Executive Vice President John Shapleigh.
Brooks said it currently is offering residential local service in Oklahoma to four of its employees on a test basis.
ALTS officials did not specify what penalty the FCC should impose on SBC, if the agency were to decide to do so. "It's the message we're looking for," said Metzger.
The FCC is expected soon to put the ALTS petition out for public comment.
"This changes nothing. We're as confident as ever in the validity of the (FCC) filing," said SBC spokesman Paul Dusseault. He said the carrier continues to believe it will win FCC approval.

SBC later Wednesday is scheduled to appeal an Oklahoma administrative law judge's finding last week that the carrier does not meet a federal checklist for long-distance entry. The appeal will be made before the three-member Oklahoma Corporation Commission.
